title: Vital signs, temperature and body measurements
blurb: Take, check and interpret observations, temperature and BMI, and know when a device reading cannot be trusted.
question: Mr Osei, 74, has atrial fibrillation. The automated machine records his blood pressure as 86/50 mmHg, yet he is warm, alert and chatting. What should the nurse do first?

teach.h: Observations are a conversation with the body
teach.body: Vital signs are the measurements that show how well the body is coping: respiration rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, level of consciousness (including new confusion) and temperature. These six are the NEWS2 parameters. A registered nurse must be able to take them manually and by device, record them accurately, and interpret them. Plain English: the number matters, the trend matters more, and the person in front of you matters most.

teach.h: Where each parameter scores 0 on NEWS2
head: Parameter
Scores 0
Scores 3
rows: New confusion, V, P or U
teach.caption: Supplemental oxygen adds 2 points. RCUK describes a normal adult respiration rate as 12–20 breaths per minute.

teach.h: When a device can mislead you
teach.body: Automated blood pressure devices may be inaccurate if the pulse is irregular, for example in atrial fibrillation. NICE NG136 says palpate the radial or brachial pulse first and, if it is irregular, measure the blood pressure manually over the brachial artery. Use a validated, maintained device and the right cuff size, with the person seated and the arm supported. Pulse oximeters can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin, and carbon monoxide can give a falsely normal reading.
teach.cite: NICE NG136 recs 1.1.2–1.1.4; NICE NG253; BTS oxygen guideline 2017 (E6)

rows.label: Main pitfall
values: Needs skill and a quiet setting

rows.label: Your check
values: Is the cuff the right size?

teach.caption: If a reading does not match how the person looks, recheck it manually and assess the person straight away.

steps.label: Lying down
steps.sub: Measure BP on their back (or seated if lying is impractical)

steps.label: Stand
steps.sub: Keep them standing for at least 1 minute

steps.label: Measure again
steps.sub: Ask about dizziness while you measure

steps.label: Compare
steps.sub: Systolic fall of 20 or more, or diastolic 10 or more

steps.label: Act
steps.sub: Review medicines, falls advice, record and report

teach.caption: NICE NG136 recs 1.1.5–1.1.6. A lying and standing BP is part of every falls assessment (NICE NG249).
Low temperature scores more than high temperature: 35.0 °C or less scores 3; 39.1 °C or more scores 2.

teach.body: Hypothermia is a body temperature below 35 °C, a medical emergency needing hospital treatment. A raised temperature is a clue, not a diagnosis: NICE NG253 warns not to rely on fever or hypothermia to rule sepsis in or out, because some people, such as older or frail people, may not develop a fever, and beta-blockers can blunt a rising heart rate. Peripheral sites such as the axilla are less accurate when the core temperature is outside 36.5–37.5 °C. Respond to the whole set of observations, not one number.
teach.cite: NHS hypothermia page; NICE NG253 recs 1.4.1–1.4.10; NICE CG65

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Adeyemi on the medical ward
items: Mrs Adeyemi, 58, of Black African heritage, is weighed at 70 kg and measured at 1.60 m on admission.
On the standard bands she would be overweight; for her background NICE uses 23–27.4 as overweight, so she is overweight but close to the obesity threshold of 27.5.
Her waist is 92 cm: 92 ÷ 160 = 0.58, increased central adiposity (0.5–0.59), so she is at increased cardiometabolic risk.
Record both, discuss them sensitively with her, and include them in her care plan.

teach.text: Two classic traps. First, 'normal' is not the same as NEWS2 zero: a pulse of 95 is within the familiar 60–100 range but scores 1 on NEWS2 (91–110). Second, an automated BP in someone with an irregular pulse is not a number to act on or dismiss: check it manually and look at the person.

items: Six NEWS2 parameters: RR, SpO2, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness (including new confusion), temperature; oxygen adds 2.
Irregular pulse: measure BP manually over the brachial artery (NICE NG136).
Postural drop: systolic 20 or more, or diastolic 10 or more, after standing at least 1 minute.
Hypothermia is below 35 °C; fever or its absence does not rule sepsis in or out.
BMI = kg ÷ m²; lower thresholds (overweight 23, obesity 27.5) for some ethnic backgrounds; waist under half height.

summary: You can now take and record vital signs manually and by device, recognise when a reading cannot be trusted, and interpret temperature, postural blood pressure and BMI against current NICE and NEWS2 bands. You know that the whole person and the trend matter more than any single number.

A.q: Mr Duarte, 70, has an irregular radial pulse. The automated machine shows a blood pressure of 96/60 mmHg and flags an error. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Measure it manually over the brachial artery
Repeat the automated reading on the other arm
Record the reading and calculate his NEWS2
Recheck with the same machine in one hour
A.why: NICE NG136 says automated devices may be inaccurate with an irregular pulse, so the blood pressure should be measured manually by auscultation over the brachial artery.

whyNot.1: Changing arms does not solve the problem: the device is unreliable because of the irregular rhythm, not the arm used.
whyNot.2: Scoring an unreliable reading could lead to the wrong response; obtain an accurate manual reading first.
whyNot.3: Waiting an hour leaves a possibly low blood pressure unconfirmed, and the same device will have the same limitation.

A.q: Ms Lewis, 31, is 1.70 m tall and weighs 52 kg. What is her BMI and how is it classified?
options: 30.6 kg/m², in the obesity class 1 range
19.2 kg/m², within the healthy weight range
18.0 kg/m², below the healthy range
20.4 kg/m², within the healthy weight range
A.why: BMI = 52 ÷ (1.70 × 1.70) = 52 ÷ 2.89 = 18.0 kg/m². This is below 18.5, which is under the healthy range and meets the NICE CG32 malnutrition criterion.

whyNot.0: 30.6 comes from dividing by height (1.70) instead of height squared.
whyNot.3: 20.4 is a miscalculation; her BMI is below 18.5, not in the healthy range.

A.q: Mr Hill, 66, is breathing air. His temperature is 35.6 °C and every other parameter scores 0. How many NEWS2 points does his temperature contribute?
options: 0 points
1 point
2 points
3 points
A.why: On NEWS2 a temperature of 35.1–36.0 °C scores 1. A total of 1 to 4 means a minimum of 4–6-hourly observations, with the registered nurse deciding on frequency or escalation.

whyNot.0: Only 36.1–38.0 °C scores 0; 35.6 °C is below that band.
whyNot.2: 2 points is given for 39.1 °C or more, not for a low reading of 35.6 °C.
whyNot.3: 3 points is for 35.0 °C or less; 35.6 °C is in the band above that.

B.q: Mrs Ahmed, 79, has had two falls. Her blood pressure lying down is 138/80 mmHg. After standing for 1 minute it is 114/76 mmHg and she feels light-headed. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: An expected drop that needs no further action
A postural drop that meets the NICE threshold
Not significant, as diastolic fell under 10 mmHg
Not valid, as she stood for less than 3 minutes
B.why: Her systolic pressure fell by 24 mmHg after standing for at least 1 minute. NICE NG136 defines a significant postural drop as a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, or a diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more.

whyNot.0: A 24 mmHg systolic fall with symptoms in someone who has fallen needs action, including a medication review.
whyNot.2: Either criterion is enough: a systolic fall of 20 or more counts even if the diastolic fall is smaller.
whyNot.3: NICE measures after standing for at least 1 minute; 3 minutes is not required.

B.q: Mr Boateng, 63, of Black African heritage, is breathless with a respiration rate of 24. His pulse oximeter reads 95% on air. Which statement best guides the nurse?
options: Oximeters tend to read low in darker skin
A saturation of 95% excludes hypoxaemia
The oximeter may overestimate his saturation
Oximetry is unreliable once RR is above 20
B.why: NICE NG253 and CG103 warn that pulse oximeters can overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, so his breathing and clinical picture must be weighed alongside the reading.

whyNot.0: The concern is overestimation (reading too high), not underestimation.
whyNot.1: One reading cannot exclude hypoxaemia, particularly when the device may overestimate and he is breathless.
whyNot.3: A raised respiration rate does not make the oximeter unreliable; it is a sign that needs scoring and assessment.

B.q: A district nurse finds Mrs Grey, 84, on her kitchen floor in winter. She is drowsy and her temperature is 34.6 °C. What is the best interpretation?
options: Mild cooling that can be managed at home
Low, but hypothermia starts under 34 °C
Normal for her age, so recheck later
Hypothermia, a medical emergency
B.why: Hypothermia is a body temperature below 35 °C and is a medical emergency needing hospital treatment. On NEWS2, 35.0 °C or less scores 3.

whyNot.0: Below 35 °C with drowsiness is hypothermia needing hospital care, not mild cooling for home management.
whyNot.1: The threshold for hypothermia is below 35 °C, not 34 °C.
whyNot.2: Age does not make 34.6 °C normal; it scores 3 on NEWS2 and she is drowsy.

C.q: Mr Patel, 68, takes bisoprolol and has a chest infection. Observations: RR 23, SpO2 95% on air, BP 98/60, pulse 84, newly confused, temperature 36.9 °C. Which statement best guides the nurse's interpretation?
options: A normal temperature makes infection unlikely
His pulse of 84 shows his circulation is stable
Bisoprolol may be blunting his heart rate rise
New confusion adds 1 point to his NEWS2
C.why: NICE NG253 warns that beta-blockers can blunt tachycardia, and that fever cannot be relied on. His RR, BP and new confusion show significant illness despite a normal pulse and temperature.

whyNot.0: NICE NG253 says do not rely on fever or its absence to rule sepsis in or out.
whyNot.1: A normal pulse on a beta-blocker can hide shock; his systolic BP of 98 already scores 2.
whyNot.3: New confusion scores 3, not 1, on NEWS2.

C.q: Mr Iqbal, 52, of Pakistani heritage, has a BMI of 28.0 kg/m². How should this be classified under NICE NG246?
options: Obesity, using the lower threshold for his background
Overweight, using the standard 25–29.9 band
Healthy weight, as his thresholds are raised by 2.5
Obesity class 2, with all thresholds cut by 5
C.why: For people of South Asian background NICE uses lower thresholds: overweight 23–27.4 and obesity 27.5 or more, so 28.0 is obesity.

whyNot.1: The standard bands do not apply to people of South Asian background; NICE says use lower thresholds.
whyNot.2: The thresholds are lowered, not raised, because cardiometabolic risk occurs at a lower BMI.
whyNot.3: Classes 2 and 3 are identified by reducing the standard thresholds by 2.5, not 5; 28.0 is obesity, not class 2.

C.q: Mr Owen, 72, is receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannulae. His SpO2 is 95%. When recording this reading, what must the record also include?
options: The probe site and the finger that was used
The oxygen device and the flow rate in use
The serial number of the pulse oximeter
His saturation after 5 minutes on room air
C.why: The BTS oxygen guideline says every record of oximetry must state whether the person is breathing air or a specified device and flow rate. On NEWS2 the oxygen itself also scores 2.

whyNot.0: Probe site may be noted locally but is not the required detail; the device and flow rate are.
whyNot.2: The device serial number is not part of the observation record.
whyNot.3: Removing prescribed oxygen to obtain an air reading is not required and could cause harm.

reteach.title: Trust the patient, then the number
reteach.question: A reading that does not fit the person in front of you is a prompt to check, not to accept or dismiss. What do you do?

blocks.body: Look at the person first. If an automated blood pressure is low but they are warm and alert, feel the pulse: if it is irregular, measure manually over the brachial artery. If saturation looks reassuring but they are breathless, remember oximeters can overestimate in darker skin. Compare against NEWS2 bands and previous readings, then act on the whole picture.

blocks.text: Hypothermia starts below 35 °C, not 36 °C: 36.0 °C is the theatre transfer threshold in NICE CG65, a different rule.

explain.body: Automated BP devices may be inaccurate with an irregular pulse, so palpate the pulse first and, if irregular, measure manually over the brachial artery (NICE NG136). Use a validated device and the correct cuff size.

items.label: the right size for the arm

test.q: Which finding should prompt the nurse to measure blood pressure manually rather than by machine?
options: A respiration rate of 22 per minute
A systolic blood pressure of 150 mmHg
A temperature of 38.2 °C
An irregularly irregular radial pulse
test.why: NICE NG136: automated devices may not measure accurately with an irregular pulse, such as atrial fibrillation, so measure manually.

whyNot.0: A raised respiration rate does not affect the accuracy of an automated BP device.
whyNot.1: A high reading alone is not a reason to change method; an irregular rhythm is.
whyNot.2: Fever does not make automated BP inaccurate.

explain.body: Hypothermia is below 35 °C and is an emergency. NEWS2 scores 35.0 °C or less as 3 and 39.1 °C or more as 2. Fever or its absence does not rule sepsis in or out (NICE NG253).

test.q: Below which body temperature is a person described as hypothermic?
options: Below 36.5 °C
Below 35 °C
Below 36 °C
Below 34 °C
test.why: Hypothermia is a body temperature below 35 °C (NHS); NEWS2 scores 35.0 °C or less as 3.

whyNot.0: 36.5 °C is the lower end of the normothermic range used in NICE CG65, not the hypothermia threshold.
whyNot.2: 36.0 °C is the NICE CG65 perioperative threshold for warming before theatre, not the definition of hypothermia.
whyNot.3: Hypothermia begins below 35 °C, so 34 °C is too low a threshold.

explain.body: Measure lying (or seated), then after standing for at least 1 minute. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more, or a diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more, is significant (NICE NG136).

test.q: When checking for postural hypotension, how long should the person stand before the second reading?
options: About 10 seconds
At least 5 minutes
At least 1 minute
At least 3 minutes
test.why: NICE NG136 rec 1.1.5: measure again after the person has been standing for at least 1 minute.

whyNot.0: 10 seconds is too short to show the postural response NICE describes.
whyNot.1: 5 minutes is longer than NICE requires and increases the falls risk for a symptomatic person.
whyNot.3: 3 minutes is used in some protocols, but NICE NG136 specifies at least 1 minute.

explain.body: BMI = kg ÷ m². Standard bands: healthy 18.5–24.9, overweight 25–29.9, obesity 30 or more. Lower thresholds (overweight 23, obesity 27.5) apply to some ethnic backgrounds. Keep the waist under half the height.

items.label: healthy waist-to-height ratio is below this

test.q: According to NICE NG246, what waist-to-height ratio should adults aim to stay below?
test.why: NICE NG246 advises keeping the waist to less than half the height, a ratio under 0.5; 0.5–0.59 is increased central adiposity.

whyNot.1: 0.6 or more is high central adiposity; risk is already increased from 0.5.
whyNot.2: 0.4 is the lower end of the healthy range, not the upper limit.
whyNot.3: 0.9 is far above the NICE limit; anything from 0.6 upwards is high central adiposity.
